seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: The Price of an Audit

blocks.text: The Bellpull Stair Reckoner leaned across the Arbor rail a minute before the stroke and smiled at me.
'I'll be calling my Audit tonight, Sandor.'

I knew the printed price. If the Arbiter weighs both jars and finds them clean, the side that called concedes two points. A Reckoner who meant to pay that would not announce it. Unless she knew something about the Ninth Stair's jar.
Her name was Hester Coyle. She had laid both hands flat on the rail, side by side, and they did not move. I watched them until the stroke.
A week earlier, in the Millrace porter's lodge, Severine Holt had asked me two questions. I answered one.
'Forty-seven,' I said.
She waited. Her hand stayed flat on her gloves. The clerk had set his chair upright and was standing behind it, holding its back with both hands.
'And who else have you told?'
I had told no one. If I said so, I would be the only person outside the Bank who knew what that jar had weighed. I did not say it.
She did not ask again. She put her gloves back on a finger at a time, the way she had taken them off.
'Irregular inflows are a liquidity matter, Miss Sandor,' she said. 'The Bank spot-checks Closes. From tonight it will check every one of yours.'

She lifted the clean jar off the counter and handed it to the clerk without looking at either of them. Then she nodded to me and went out. She had not raised her voice. She had told me what would happen, not what she would do.
The clerk sat down again. He wrote something in the margin of his book, blotted it and closed the book on his own fingers before he took them out. He did not look at me while I signed for the jar.

I knew the printed rule. The Bank can refuse a key. It cannot take back a key it has confirmed. Only the Arbiters' Court can do that, for a proven offence, at an open hearing. I had read it at Whitlow's table, and I read it again that night at the Guild desk with my key locked in the drawer under my hand.

I took out my notebook and read the figures I had copied at the first Close: three hundred, two hundred and twenty-three, seventy-seven, a hundred and twenty-four, forty-seven over. They were the same figures they had been. Nobody had asked me for the notebook.
I wanted to stop being afraid of a Bank that could not touch my licence. I was still afraid.

Lisle's stalls came at three in the morning, every night of that week, twenty-one minutes each, while she slept. Each morning she woke. Her foreman's book had nothing new in it. Drewe's stalls came at half past one, while she slept, and on the third afternoon at ten past three she stalled behind her family's counter for twenty minutes and nobody came in.
'Shop was very quiet,' she told me. 'Even for us. I was the quietest thing in it.'
On the afternoon of the match she came up the Ninth Stair with her fist closed and opened it over my hand. Two coppers.
'Woke up,' she said. 'Seven times. Don't make a thing of it.'
I did not make a thing of it. I put them in my coat.

She did not bet on anything else that afternoon. She stood at the landing window with her arms folded while Drewe and Tran read the Rate Board, and when Drewe made a pun about it she did not answer. My verdict was that she was nervous about Bellpull.
I asked what they knew about Bellpull's Reckoner. Lisle shrugged. Drewe knew.
'Coyle,' she said. 'Banks like she's buying a house. Big early, then nothing. Everybody says so.'
I did not know whether everybody was right. It was not anything I could read in the printed Laws. I wrote it down, and I wrote down beside it that I had heard it from Drewe.
Tran drank his black chicory from the stone jug and read the Rate Board over Drewe's shoulder.

The League Rater had posted the Rate Board for our landing at midnight. Both Hour plates at true rate. V and VII at double. Everything else true. There was no plate like Millrace's XII, nothing for a two-spender run to beat.
'Put me back on winding,' Drewe said. She was turning her screwdriver over and over. 'Sprinting's the wrong train for me. My knees have lodged a complaint.'
'Mm,' Tran said. 'She winds clean.'

I lodged the sheet that afternoon: Lisle Sprinter, Tran Stiller and Keep on XII, Drewe Winder. Ninth Stair at home, defending XII. My verdict on Drewe was that she wanted her old place back, and I saw no reason she should not have it.

So when Coyle leaned on the rail and promised me her Audit, I thought about what she could know. The Bank's ruling on our first jar was in the Bank's books. The Governor had stood in a porter's lodge and asked who else I had told. My verdict was that Coyle was not bluffing. Nobody makes that threat in front of an Arbiter without a reason.
Tran had heard her from plate XII.
'Loud ones don't call,' he said. 'Mm. Usually.'
I did not know whether that was true. It is not in the printed Laws, and I did not count on it.

There was nothing in the printed Laws I could do about another Reckoner's Audit except keep my own jar honest. I could weigh it on the Arbor scale in any Bank minute, and the reading would be mine alone. But Coyle would watch me do it, and a Reckoner who weighs her own jar after a threat is a Reckoner who is not sure of it.
So I left the threat alone and played the slates.
The stroke came. The Arbiter set the jars on the Arbor, one each side of the rail, three hundred seconds in each.

Round one started on plate I, one stride from our Hour plate. Bellpull ran it. I saw nothing, as I never do. When I could see again, their Sprinter, a thin man called Ferrier, was standing on XII with empty hands, and the Token lay by Tran's boot. Bellpull's Tally read ten spent.
'Sprung,' Tran told me afterwards. 'He was slow. I wasn't.'

Coyle's first slate was sixty. Mine was nothing. Her second was fifty, her third forty, her fourth thirty. Drewe had been right about the house. I wrote nothing each time, because every second I banked against her was a second Lisle could not spend. Lisle ran from the far starts in rounds two, three and four and was Spilled in each: twice on V, by a Stiller who held the double plate, and once on VI, by a Keep who stood in the middle of her plate and waited.
'Lisle, forty.'
'Held.'

Each time I saw nothing, and each time the Token was somewhere new and Lisle was standing over it with her hands open, and the Tally had moved. She called her spends back to me across the ring when she could: thirty-eight, thirty-one, twenty-two. I wrote them in the margin of my sheet, for the Stall Book.
'Their wall's on V,' she said after round three. 'Their Keep doesn't come to you. She waits.' She did not make a bet of it.

By the fourth Bank minute Bellpull had a hundred and eighty seconds locked in their bank chamber and led four to nothing. Four points is two more than an Audit costs. My verdict was that Coyle was buying the price before she called. I kept that verdict, and I kept my jar.
Her slates had gone sixty, fifty, forty, thirty. The Tally said her jar held a hundred and ten. If she kept falling by ten, her next slate was twenty.
Round five started on plate V, one stride from Bellpull's Hour plate.
'Lisle, thirty.'
'Held.'

Then the landing was different. The Token was on VI, flat on the rim nearest V, and Lisle was standing over it with her fist up. Bellpull's Keep was on her knees beside her with one hand on Lisle's shoulder. The Arbiter, with his Fob on its chain, ruled the Token had left Lisle's hand before the Keep's hand reached her. Two points.
'She stands in the middle and waits for you to come to her,' Lisle said afterwards. 'Round four I went to her. This time I didn't. Front foot on the rim and down.'
She called her spend across to me from the plate, the way she had after every run. 'Nine.'
I wrote it in the margin with the others, for the Stall Book.
Coyle wrote twenty in that Bank minute. I wrote twenty-one. In round six she wrote ten and I wrote eleven. Level at four.
In round seven she wrote nothing, and I wrote one.

She had stopped banking. Her jar was kept for something. I wrote one in round eight, and she wrote nothing, and the points came to us a second at a time. Lisle was Spilled on VI in round six, on VI again in round seven and on VII in round eight, where their Stiller had moved to the other double plate. We led six to four.
Then the Tokens started on IX, X and XI, coming round towards our Hour plate, and Coyle spent what she had kept.

In round nine Ferrier ran from IX. I issued Lisle fifteen to meet him. She spent on his breath, inside his Lull, and put a hand on his arm on XI. The Token lay dead on XI when I could see again. Coyle wrote nothing in that Bank minute, and I wrote one. Seven to four.

In round ten Bellpull put their Winder on the dead floor at the rim of XII, on the XI side, standing still as a post. Dead floor is nobody's plate. Ferrier came round behind him and placed. In round eleven they did it again from one plate out. I issued Lisle fifteen each time, because I would rather lose seconds than points. Lisle spent twelve each time and could not reach him. You cannot pass through a frozen man, and the printed rule would not let her onto XII while Tran stood on it.
'She put the big one by my plate,' Tran told me. He was standing very straight, and he said it slowly, the way he says everything. 'Ferrier came round the back of him. I was at the front. Slow.'
I wrote one in round ten and won it. In round eleven Coyle wrote one too. Equal banks score nothing. She had been reading my slates the way I had been reading hers.
Eight points each, into round twelve.
Drewe came to the edge of the Arbor in that Bank minute, as near as a player may, turning her screwdriver over. 'Level,' she said. 'Like a well-set balance. Nobody panic.'
Lisle did not come. She stayed on XI with her arms folded and looked at the plate under her feet.
Round twelve's Token starts on plate XII. Our Hour plate. Bellpull's target. To score, they had to carry it off and back on.

I read the Tally. Ours: two hundred and ten spent, thirty-seven banked. By the Tally our jar held fifty-three. Theirs: forty-five spent, two hundred and eleven banked. By the Tally theirs held forty-four. I had added Coyle's slates all night as they were shown, and the sum matched the Tally's banked column to the second.
If Bellpull did not score, I could out-bank anything Coyle had left. She could do that sum as easily as I could. She had to run.

The printed rule is one player from each team on a plate. Ferrier had to stand on XII to lift the Token, and step back onto it to score. So their Winder could not stand there with him, and a screen on the dead floor would not keep Ferrier off Tran's plate. Tran would have his plate to himself, and only one man to stop.

I worked out what I could issue Lisle and still be sure of the slate, however little Ferrier spent. Nine. Nine seconds would cover one side of XII. Tran's plate covered both, and in the last two rounds Lisle had spent twenty-four seconds and not reached a man near XII.
I kept the nine. I issued nothing.
Lisle, on XI, looked across the ring at me and held up an empty hand. I shook my head. She put her hand down and stood with her feet apart, watching Ferrier, and said nothing.
'Ferrier, twenty,' Coyle said.
'Held.'
When I could see again, Ferrier was standing on I with his hands at his sides, and the Token lay on XII by Tran's boot. Bellpull's Tally read fifty-six spent.
'Picked it up,' Tran said. 'Went off to One. Came back. I was there. He walked back to One on what he had left.'

The Arbiter ruled it a Spill on XII. A dead Token, and in live play Ferrier could not touch it for five seconds. When they were up, he looked at it and did not move. The round ran out with the Token where it lay.
The Bank minute opened. I did the sum once and checked it once. Fifty-six spent, two hundred and eleven banked. If Coyle's jar was honest, it could not hold more than thirty-three.
I wrote thirty-four.
The Arbiter turned the slates over together.
'Ninth Stair thirty-four,' he said. 'Bellpull thirty-three.'
The bank point was ours. Nine to eight.
On plate XI Lisle put both fists in the air and did not say anything at all. Drewe, on VII, said, 'Won by a hairspring.' Tran sat down on his plate where he stood.
Eleven points. Out of the bottom two. Before my first midnight the Ninth Stair had been last, on four.
Coyle was not looking at the Tally. She was looking at me. Her hands were back on the rail, flat, and she still had her Audit, and the minute was not over.

By the printed table it would cost her nothing now. A loss by one and a loss by three are the same loss. Nothing I did with my hands could change what an Audit cost her, so I did what I had not done all night. I lifted our jar in both hands, barehanded, and checked the empty pan of the Arbor scale read zero. Then I set the jar on it. The dial faced me.
Issue three hundred. Tally spent two hundred and ten. The jar should hold ninety: thirty-four and thirty-seven in the bank chamber, nineteen loose.
It read a hundred and twenty-five.
The glass was warm under my hands, like a cup someone had just put down.

I had written Lisle's spends in the margin all night as she called them, for the Stall Book. I had not added them. There had been no time. I added them now. Two hundred and five. The Tally said two hundred and ten. The Tally counts every spend and every Winder's friction. Five seconds of our Tally were friction, and I had not issued Drewe one second to wind all night. Five seconds of friction on seconds I never issued.

The other thirty had come back into the jar at the ends of rounds, with Lisle's held seconds, and I had never issued them. In every round Lisle had spent less than I issued her. She had not spent a second that was not hers. Thirty, and five. Thirty-five over.

The printed WINDING rule is plain. A Winder touching catch-brass and a teammate at once can wind the brass's seconds into the teammate. Only a Winder can do it, and only in live play, between Lulls. The friction is charged to her.
Tonight the Ninth Stair had one Winder. At our first Close, when the jar was warm, we had had one Winder too.

I thought of the brass box Drewe turned over and over in her fingers on the landing. I had decided it was her gran's. I did not know any more whether I had decided right. Warm seconds come from someone's waiting within the last day. I did not know whose.
If Coyle called now, the Arbiter would weigh my jar against the Tally and find thirty-five over. Pool Fraud. The match forfeited, and the eleven points back to eight.
I was afraid. I looked at Drewe. She was still on VII, laughing at something Lisle had shouted across the ring, and her hands were in her coat pockets.

Then I looked at Coyle's hands. She had lifted one off the rail and was holding it there, open, a little above the brass. She was not looking at the scale or the slates. She was looking at my face, and the minute was not over.
